subject: chemistry-2
question: A laboratory solution is prepared by dissolving 5 g of sodium chloride in 95 g of water. Which term correctly identifies the water in this mixture, and what mass of it is present?

options.text: The solute, 5 g, because it is the component dispersed throughout the mixture
The solvent, 5 g, because it is the component that is no longer visible
The solute, 95 g, because it establishes the final volume of the mixture
The solvent, 95 g, because it is the component present in greater amount and does the dissolving

explanation:
In a solution the solvent is the component present in the greatest amount and it disperses the solute to the level of individual particles or ions; here water (95 g) is the solvent and NaCl (5 g) is the solute. The total solution mass is 100 g, so 100 g minus the 5 g of solute leaves 95 g of solvent. Identifying solute versus solvent correctly is the first step in every concentration calculation, because concentration is always some measure of solute relative to either the solvent or the total solution.

ELI-10: Two jobs exist in any solution: one substance does the dissolving and one substance gets dissolved. The dissolver is the solvent, and it is normally the component you have far more of; the dissolved substance is the solute. Here the numbers decide it for you: 95 g of water against 5 g of salt, so water is the solvent. Note that the salt does not vanish when it disappears from view, it has simply spread out as separate sodium and chloride ions too small to see.
